books.section: The New Left, Feminism, and the Counterculture

primary_sources: Dr. Benjamin Spock, The Common Sense Book of Baby and Child Care (1946)
Jimmy Carter, 'Crisis of Confidence' speech, July 15, 1979

source: original; documents are paraphrases of public sources (see each document's sourcing note); images are public-domain or licensed photographs viewed before writing

stimulus.source_note: DBQ: documents below are the stimulus.

prompt: Evaluate the extent to which American culture changed between 1945 and 1980.

documents.title: Television ownership
documents.source: U.S. Census Bureau, Statistical Abstract, table HS-42.
documents.sourcing: Government data on how fast television spread, showing the rise of a shared mass medium.
documents.text: Share of American households owning at least one television set: 1950, 9.0 percent; 1955, 64.5 percent; 1960, 87.1 percent.

documents.title: Advice for new parents
documents.source: Dr. Benjamin Spock, The Common Sense Book of Baby and Child Care (1946). Paraphrased.
documents.sourcing: A pediatrician's best-selling guide, written for the millions of parents of the baby boom.
documents.text: Spock told parents to trust their own judgment, writing that 'you know more than you think you do.' He called child-rearing a natural process and urged a relaxed, permissive approach instead of strict schedules and harsh discipline.

documents.title: The new rock star
documents.source: Photograph: Elvis Presley, 1956 publicity portrait. Public domain (published in the United States in 1956 without a copyright notice), via Wikimedia Commons.
documents.sourcing: A publicity portrait of the singer who carried rock 'n' roll to a mass audience.
documents.text: The photograph shows a young Elvis Presley with slicked-back hair, a white singer from Memphis, Tennessee, who became the most famous performer of the new rock 'n' roll music.

documents.title: On the road
documents.source: Jack Kerouac, On the Road (1957). Paraphrased.
documents.sourcing: A Beat novel celebrating travel and freedom, written against suburban and consumer life.
documents.text: Kerouac's novel follows two friends driving across America, living by spontaneity and freedom. The Beats rejected the suburban lifestyle, the consumer society, and cold war patriotism, and they praised jazz, travel, and Eastern spirituality.

documents.title: The problem that has no name
documents.source: Betty Friedan, The Feminine Mystique (1963). Paraphrased.
documents.sourcing: A book naming the dissatisfaction of suburban housewives, written to start a movement.
documents.text: Friedan wrote that many suburban housewives felt a deep dissatisfaction they could not name. These women had homes, husbands, and children, yet they felt empty and asked, in effect, 'Is this all?'

documents.title: Woodstock
documents.source: Photograph: crowd at the Woodstock Music Festival, August 15, 1969. Photograph by Derek Redmond and Paul Campbell, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
documents.sourcing: A photograph of the festival crowd, showing the counterculture gathered at its largest.
documents.text: The photograph shows part of the huge crowd at the Woodstock Music Festival on a dairy farm in Bethel, New York. More than 400,000 young people gathered for three days of rock music.

documents.title: A crisis of confidence
documents.source: President Jimmy Carter, televised address, July 15, 1979. Paraphrased.
documents.sourcing: A president speaking to the nation on television, describing a mood of doubt after a decade of shocks.
documents.text: Carter said the nation faced a crisis of confidence, a sense that Americans no longer believed their country could solve its problems. He said the crisis came from doubting the meaning of American life, and he urged a return to faith, family, and hard work.

rubric.criterion: Thesis: earns the point for a historically defensible claim that answers the prompt, stating the extent to which American culture changed between 1945 and 1980, with a clear line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: Restating the prompt with no claim about the extent of cultural change does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Contextualization: earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as postwar prosperity and the baby boom, the Cold War, or the social movements of the 1960s.
rubric.notEarned: A sentence of background with no link to the argument, or background from a later century, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (first point): earns the point for describing specific and relevant content from at least three documents, such as television ownership, Spock's advice, or Friedan's book.
rubric.notEarned: Naming documents without describing their content does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (second point): earns the point for using the content of at least six documents to support an argument about cultural change.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or quoting documents without connecting them to the argument, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence beyond the documents: earns the point for describing a specific and relevant example beyond the documents, such as the Beats, abstract expressionism, the birth control pill, or the conservative backlash of the 1970s.
rubric.notEarned: A general statement about culture with no specific example does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Sourcing: earns the point for explaining the relevance of a document's author, purpose, audience, or historical situation for at least two documents, such as Friedan's purpose in starting a movement or Carter's purpose in speaking to a doubtful nation.
rubric.notEarned: Describing what a document says without explaining why its source matters does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Complexity: earns the point for demonstrating a complex understanding, such as qualifying the thesis by period, explaining why change was deep in some areas and shallow in others, or weighing the mass culture against the dissent it provoked.
rubric.notEarned: A second example with no qualification or weighing does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: American culture changed deeply between 1945 and 1980, as a shared mass culture formed and then broke open into rebellion and doubt, though the pull of conformity and traditional values never disappeared.
Context: Postwar prosperity, the baby boom, and the Cold War made the 1950s a decade of suburbs, television, and pressure to fit in.
Evidence: Documents 1 and 2 show the new mass culture forming, through television in nearly every home and expert advice guiding new parents. Documents 3, 4, and 5 show the challenges, through rock 'n' roll, Beat writing, and Friedan's attack on the housewife ideal. Document 6 shows the counterculture at its peak at Woodstock, and Document 7 shows the decade ending in doubt, with Carter naming a crisis of confidence.
Outside evidence: Abstract expressionism broke from realistic art, the birth control pill helped change attitudes toward sex, and the conservative backlash of the 1970s pushed back toward traditional values.
Complexity: The change was real but uneven. Mass culture spread fast in the 1950s, rebellion spread fast in the 1960s, and by the 1970s both the rebels and their critics doubted the country, so the extent of change looks different in each decade.
